lesson_title: The Biggest Kraal: Optimisation and Rates of Change
hook_text: One roll of fence, one farm wall. What's the biggest kraal you can build? Calculus answers without a single guess.
clip_script: You have 120 metres of fencing and a long farm wall to build against. Fence a skinny sliver — it holds nothing. Fence a strip so deep the wire runs out on the sides — also nothing. Somewhere between the two silly extremes hides the biggest kraal, and calculus walks straight to it. Call the width x. The wall gives you one side free, so the front gets 120 minus two x. Area: x times that — a frowning parabola, zero at both extremes, biggest at the top of the frown. And the top of any curve is where its slope is zero. Differentiate: 120 minus four x. Set to zero: x is 30. Width 30, front 60 — 1800 square metres, and no trial and error anywhere. Doubt it? Try 29 or 31 and watch the area dip on both sides. That is the whole optimisation chapter: write the thing you want as a formula, use the fixed fact to get down to one letter, find the flat spot. Same recipe designs the cheapest tin, the fastest route, the biggest profit. The derivative doesn't just draw graphs — it makes decisions.
visual_style: A farm at golden hour, fence posts snapping into place along a wall, silly extreme kraals collapsing, an area curve rising over the field with a ball settling at its flat peak, the winning 30 by 60 kraal drawing itself.
pacing: Playful on the failed designs, steady through the setup, a decisive snap when the derivative lands on 30.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and let the derivative make the best decision every time.
